sections.title: A promise represents a later result
sections.body: A promise begins pending and later becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. then registers success work, catch registers rejection work, and finally runs cleanup that should not depend on the result. Calling then returns a new promise, which is why chains can transform values and propagate errors.

sections.title: A chain follows returned values
sections.body: A then callback can return a normal value for the next step or return a promise that the chain waits for. Forgetting to return an inner promise starts detached work, so later errors and completion are no longer connected to the chain. Add one final catch where recovery or reporting belongs.

sections.title: await pauses one async function
sections.body: An async function always returns a promise. await pauses that async function until the awaited promise settles; it does not block the whole JavaScript runtime. Independent operations can begin together and be awaited with Promise.all, while dependent operations should remain ordered.

sections.title: try, catch, and finally
sections.body: try/catch around awaited work can handle a rejection. Catch an error only when you can recover, add useful context, or report it; otherwise rethrow it. finally is useful for cleanup such as clearing a loading flag, and it runs whether the operation succeeds or fails.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Promises, async/await, and errors is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain promises, async/await, and errors to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Explain pending, fulfilled, and rejected promises. Return promises from chains. Use async and await as promise syntax. Handle errors at a useful boundary.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using promises, async/await, and errors behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can promises, async/await, and errors affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using promises, async/await, and errors produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
